# Vesicoureteral reflux

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Urologic surgery > Vesicoureteral reflux*

[Original Article Link](/library/-i0D8f)

---

## Summary

Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is the retrograde flow of urine from the <u>bladder</u> into the <u>ureter</u>. <u>Primary VUR</u> is the most common type and is due to a developmental anomaly of the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ). <u>Secondary VUR</u> is caused by <u>bladder outlet obstruction</u>, congenital ureteral anomalies, or voiding dysfunction (e.g., <u>neurogenic bladder</u>). Children with VUR are usually asymptomatic or may present with a <u>febrile urinary tract infection</u> (<u>UTI</u>). Other manifestations include <u>hypertension</u>, <u>uremia</u>, and <u>kidney failure</u> in advanced cases of <u>reflux nephropathy</u>. VUR is diagnosed based on <u>voiding cystourethrography</u> findings. Treatment includes surveillance, continuous <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>, and/or <u>surgery</u> and is based on VUR grade, risk for <u>kidney injury</u>, and likelihood of spontaneous resolution. Children with VUR often have associated <u>bladder and bowel dysfunction</u> (BBD), which decreases the likelihood of spontaneous resolution and should be assessed for and treated. Complications of VUR include <u>hydronephrosis</u>, <u>pyelonephritis</u>, and <u>chronic kidney disease</u> (<u>CKD</u>).

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u> 

* ∼ 2 % of all <u>newborns</u>

* Approx. 40% of children with a <u>UTI</u>

* Approx. 15% of <u>infants</u> with antenatally diagnosed <u>hydronephrosis</u> [[1]](/library/uhVpf80)[[2]](/library/fRVkm80)

* <u>Prevalence</u> decreases with age.  [[3]](/library/gXVFxG0)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: children < 2 years of age [[4]](/library/Z9XZNZ0)

* Sex 

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> in children < 2 years of age

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> in older children

* Race: more common in White children than Black children




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### <u>Primary VUR</u> (most common type)




* Developmental anomaly of the vesicoureteric junction (VUJ): short intramural <u>ureter</u> → VUJ fails to close completely during <u>bladder</u> contraction → VUR

* A hereditary component is likely.  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)





![Primary vesicoureteral reflux - pathomechanism](media/vcqynsvog1m7ulg09p8ymk4z.jpg)

Primary vesicoureteral reflux - pathomechanism




### <u>Secondary VUR</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




* <u>Bladder outlet obstruction</u>: high pressure within the <u>bladder</u> → reflux of urine through the VUJ

* Anatomical (e.g., <u>posterior urethral valves</u>, urethral <u>meatal stenosis</u>)

* Functional (e.g., <u>neurogenic bladder</u>)

* Congenital anomalies of the <u>ureter</u>

* <u>Duplex collecting system</u>: most common congenital renal abnormality (affects ∼ 1% of the population)   [[6]](/library/thVXf80)

* <u>Ectopic ureter</u>

* <u>Ureterocele</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u>: following <u>surgery</u> that involves the <u>vesical trigone</u> (e.g., transurethral <u>bladder</u> operations); <u>renal transplant</u> <u>surgery</u> [[7]](/library/YRVnl80)[[8]](/library/bRVHl80)

## Clinical features

* Suspected in the prenatal period when <u>hydronephrosis</u> is detected on routine antenatal <u>ultrasound</u>

* Postnatal presentation

* Recurrent <u>febrile</u> <u>urinary tract infections</u>

* <u>Neonates</u>: irritability, <u>fever</u>

* Older children: <u>urinary urgency</u>, frequency, incontinence, and <u>dysuria</u> associated with <u>fever</u>

* See also "<u>Clinical features of UTI in children</u>."

* <u>Reflux nephropathy</u>

* Flank or abdominal <u>pain</u> before or during voiding





> [!TIP]
> VUR is generally asymptomatic until it causes a <u>urinary tract infection</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)[[9]](/library/20VT2G0)[[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)




* VUR is typically diagnosed through either of the following:

* <u>Diagnostics for pediatric UTI</u>

* Follow-up of <u>antenatally detected hydronephrosis</u>

* Imaging is necessary to confirm <u>diagnosis of VUR</u>.

* <u>Renal and bladder ultrasound</u> (<u>RBUS</u>) is typically performed as initial imaging to assess for structural abnormalities, but it is not diagnostic.

* <u>Voiding cystourethrography</u> (<u>VCUG</u>) is the <u>gold standard</u> for diagnosis.  [[1]](/library/uhVpf80)[[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> and additional imaging are indicated to assess for: 

* Complications (e.g., <u>UTI</u>, <u>kidney failure</u>)

* An underlying cause and/or associated BBD





### Imaging




#### <u>RBUS</u> [[9]](/library/20VT2G0)[[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)[[11]](/library/um1phh0)




* Indications 

* Selected patients with <u>UTI</u>: See "<u>Imaging for pediatric UTI</u>."  [[9]](/library/20VT2G0)[[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)

* Postnatal follow-up of antenatally detected <u>urinary tract</u> dilation  [[1]](/library/uhVpf80)

* Findings suggestive of VUR include: [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* <u>Hydronephrosis</u>

* Ureteral dilation

* Changes to the renal <u>parenchyma</u>

* Asymmetric <u>kidney</u> size

* <u>Bladder</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>bladder</u> wall thickening)

* Congenital anomalies (e.g., duplex <u>kidney</u>)





> [!TIP]
> <u>RBUS</u> has low <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> for detecting VUR. Normal findings on <u>RBUS</u> do not rule out VUR. [[11]](/library/um1phh0)




![Hydronephrosis](media/fkyc2qx0ajxhg0ogerg06qmu.jpg)

Hydronephrosis




#### VUR imaging [[1]](/library/uhVpf80)[[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




* Indications [[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)[[11]](/library/um1phh0)

* Findings suggestive of VUR on <u>RBUS</u>

* Any of the following (regardless of <u>RBUS</u> findings) 

* Atypical or complicated <u>pediatric UTI</u>

* Recurrent <u>febrile UTI</u>

* Modalities

* <u>VCUG</u>: <u>gold standard</u> [[1]](/library/uhVpf80)[[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Voiding urosonography: a radiation-free alternative to <u>VCUG</u> that uses a microbubble contrast to evaluate for VUR and associated renal anomalies  [[9]](/library/20VT2G0)[[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)

* Radionuclide cystography: uses a radioactive tracer (e.g., <u>Tc-99m MAG3</u>) to evaluate for VUR [[12]](/library/TRV6m80)

* May be considered as an alternative to <u>VCUG</u> in girls  [[9]](/library/20VT2G0)

* Toilet-trained children may not require catheterization.

* Findings [[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)

* Retrograde flow of contrast into the <u>ureters</u>

* Visualization of <u>urinary tract</u> dilation and congenital anomalies of the <u>urinary tract</u>

* See also "<u>VUR grading</u>".





#### Other imaging




* <u>DMSA scan</u>: may be considered in selected patients to assess <u>kidney function</u> and evaluate for renal scarring  [[10]](/library/f0Vk2G0)[[11]](/library/um1phh0)

* <u>Urodynamic testing</u>: may be used to evaluate patients with <u>secondary VUR</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




Indicated in all patients as part of the initial assessment.




* <u>Urinalysis</u> and <u>urine culture</u>: to evaluate for <u>pediatric UTI</u>

* <u>Kidney function tests</u>: to assess for <u>kidney</u> disease

---

## Treatment

The goal of VUR management is to prevent complications (e.g., recurrent <u>febrile UTI</u>, <u>reflux nephropathy</u>).




### Approach [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




* All patients

* Refer patients to specialists (e.g., urology) for management.

* Identify and treat associated complications, e.g.:

* <u>UTI</u>

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Proteinuria</u>

* For <u>secondary VUR</u>, treat the underlying cause.

* Children 

* Choice of management depends on several factors, including the likelihood of spontaneous resolution and patient and/or family preference.  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* VUR grades I and II without complications: typically managed with surveillance or continuous <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>

* VUR grade ≥ 4 and/or complications: <u>Surgery</u> may be indicated.

* Adults [[3]](/library/gXVFxG0)

* There is insufficient evidence on <u>management of VUR</u> in adults.

* <u>Surgery</u> may be considered for adults with VUR and <u>recurrent UTIs</u> and/or <u>pyelonephritis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> VUR often resolves spontaneously, especially in children with <u>primary VUR</u> grades I or II. [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




> [!TIP]
> There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening of asymptomatic family members of patients with VUR. Educate family members on the increased risk for VUR and the need for prompt evaluation of <u>UTI symptoms</u>. [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




### <u>Conservative management</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




#### Surveillance




* Surveillance alone may be considered in children with lower grade VUR, low risk for recurrent <u>febrile UTIs</u>, and no known renal scarring.

* Educate caregivers on the <u>symptoms of pediatric UTI</u> and need for prompt <u>treatment of pediatric UTI</u>.

* Identify and treat BBD: voiding behavior modification, <u>treatment of pediatric constipation</u>

* <u>Circumcision</u> of male <u>infants</u> with VUR may be considered to decrease the risk of <u>UTIs</u>; use <u>shared decision-making</u>. [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Serially monitor the following to assess for complications and disease status:  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Weight and height

* Blood pressure

* <u>Kidney function tests</u>

* Imaging, e.g.: [[9]](/library/20VT2G0)

* <u>RBUS</u> to assess <u>kidney</u> growth and scarring

* VUR imaging for progression or resolution of VUR

* <u>DMSA scan</u> as indicated for follow-up of abnormal imaging findings or other concerns for scarring





> [!TIP]
> Up to 50% of <u>infants</u> and children with VUR have BBD, which increases the risk for complications and decreases the likelihood of spontaneous resolution of VUR.




#### Continuous <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>




* In addition to surveillance, consider continuous <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u> in:  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Children < 1 year of age

* Children with VUR grade IV or V and/or <u>risk factors for pediatric UTI</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Children with <u>febrile UTI</u> during surveillance

* Options: low-dose <u>trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole</u>, <u>amoxicillin</u>, <u>nitrofurantoin</u> [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Duration: tailored to the individual  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)





### <u>Surgery</u>




* Indications [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Persistent grade IV or V VUR [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Breakthrough <u>febrile UTIs</u> despite continuous <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>

* Noncompliance with long-term prophylactic <u>antibiotics</u>

* New renal scarring

* Patient and/or family preference

* Options [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* Endoscopic subureteric transurethral injection  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* <u>Ureteroneocystostomy</u> (<u>ureteral reimplantation</u>)  [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)





> [!TIP]
> After <u>surgery</u>, follow up with patients through <u>adolescence</u> to evaluate for complications of VUR and assess <u>kidney function</u>. [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)




> [!TIP]
> Treat BBD (voiding behavior modification, <u>treatment of constipation</u>) and monitor for resolution of VUR before considering surgical <u>management of VUR</u>.

---

## Complications

* Infections [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* <u>Urosepsis</u>

* <u>Pyelonephritis</u>

* <u>Perinephric abscess</u>

* Renal complications [[5]](/library/U0Vb2G0)

* <u>Megaureter</u>

* <u>Hydronephrosis</u>

* Reflux nephropathy: renal scarring due to VUR [[15]](/library/XRV9l80) 

* Patients are often asymptomatic.

* Can lead to <u>hypertension</u>, <u>chronic kidney disease</u> and, rarely, <u>end-stage kidney disease</u> [[16]](/library/cRVaN80)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
